subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: In this unit you will go further with halves. You will say what a half really means — one of two equal parts — and check that the two halves are equal. You will halve shapes by folding, cutting and drawing, share a group of objects into two equal halves, halve small even numbers, and read the symbol ½.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 1 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Say that a half is one of two equal parts of a whole.
Understand that the two halves must be equal in size or amount.
Tell the difference between equal parts and unequal parts.
Fold or draw a line to cut a shape into two halves.
See that a shape can often be halved in more than one way.
Put two halves back together to remake the whole.
Share a small group of objects equally between two to find half of a set.
Find half of small even numbers: half of 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.
Recognise and say the symbol ½ as ‘one half’.

concepts.title: What a Half Really Means (two equal parts)
concepts.explanation: The whole unit rests on one idea: a half is one of two equal parts. Not just two parts — two equal parts. It is easy to break a biscuit into a big bit and a tiny bit and call them ‘halves’, because there are two pieces. Your job all week is to keep returning to the word equal: the two pieces must be the same size, so that it is fair.
concepts.example: Look at that two halves make the whole again. Pour a full cup of water into two equal cups — ‘half here, half here’ — then pour both back into one cup: ‘the whole is back.’ This back-and-forth, whole to halves to whole, is a powerful picture and worth repeating with different things: a folded paper opened flat again, two half-mangoes held together, two halves of a cake pushed back into a circle.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Take one piece of anjero (or a paper circle) and say, ‘This is one whole.’ Fold it carefully down the middle so the two sides sit exactly on top of each other, then open it. ‘Look — two parts, and they are the same size. Each one is a half.’ Then deliberately tear a second circle into a big part and a small part and ask, ‘Are these two halves?’ The child will tell you they are not, because they are not equal. Comparing a true half with a false one, side by side, is the fastest way to fix the idea. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “I have one whole anjero. Watch me fold it. Do the two sides match?” Child: “Yes, they are the same.” You: “So each part is a half. Half plus half makes one whole.” You (tearing a big bit and a small bit): “Are these halves?” Child: “No — one is bigger!” You: “Well spotted. Halves must be equal. That means the same size, so it is fair.” Link the idea straight to fairness and sharing, which the child already understands deeply. ‘If I share my dates with you, we each want the same. That is a half for you and a half for me.’ Fairness gives the maths a reason you care about. Return to it often: when a snack is split, when a toy is shared, when juice is poured, quietly name the half.

concepts.title: Halves of Shapes (fold, cut and draw a line)
concepts.explanation: Now you halve shapes. The surprising part is that a shape can often be cut in half in more than one way, and every correct way still makes two equal parts. A circle can be halved with a line straight down, straight across, or slanted — as long as the line goes through the middle. A square or rectangle can be halved down the middle the tall way, the wide way, or corner to corner.
concepts.grownUpGuide:
How to teach it: Folding is your best friend here, because a fold that matches exactly proves the two parts are equal. Give the child a paper square. ‘Fold it so the two parts sit exactly on top of each other.’ When it matches, open it and draw a line along the crease — ‘that line shows the two halves.’ Then take a fresh square and ask, ‘Can you find a different fold that also makes two equal halves?’ Collect two or three different ways and lay them out together. One idea gently stretches you: the two halves must be equal in size, but they do not have to be the same shape to look at. If you cut a square from corner to corner you get two triangles; they look different from the two rectangles you get by folding down the middle, yet each way still gives two equal halves of the same square. You do not need to labour this — simply see and feel, by folding and matching, that both ways are fair.

🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Here is a paper circle. Fold it so both sides match. Do they?” Child: “Yes!” You: “Then each side is a half. Draw a line on the fold.” You: “Now fold it a different way — up and down instead of side to side. Does it still match?” Child: “Yes, still the same.” You: “Clever — a circle has lots of ways to make two halves.”

concepts.title: Half of a Set (share a group equally between two)
concepts.explanation: A half is not only for shapes — it works for groups of objects too. To find half of a set, you share the group equally between two. Each of the two groups then holds the same number, and that number is ‘half of’ the whole set. This is where halves connect to counting, which you already know well.
concepts.example: Give this idea a gentle real-world story you will recognise. ‘Jamil needs half of these eggs for his cakes and Sairah needs half for her cookies. Let us share them fairly so each gets the same.’ Sharing between two brothers and sisters, between two plates at iftar, or between two friends turns ‘half of a set’ into something you do happily every day.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Put out 6 dates. Give the child two plates. ‘Share the dates fairly — one for this plate, one for that plate, one for this plate…’ Deal them out one at a time, back and forth, until they are gone. Then count one plate: ‘Three dates. So half of 6 is 3.’ Dealing one-to-each is the most reliable method for a young child, far surer than trying to split the pile by eye. Practise with 2, 4, 8 and 10 objects, always by dealing back and forth. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Here are 8 stones and two cloths. Let us share them fairly between two.” You and child (dealing): “One for you, one for me, one for you, one for me…” You: “Now count one group. How many?” Child: “Four.” You: “So half of 8 is 4. Both groups are equal — that is fair.”

concepts.title: Halving Small Even Numbers
concepts.explanation: From sharing real objects, you move to halving numbers: half of 2 is 1, half of 4 is 2, half of 6 is 3, half of 8 is 4, half of 10 is 5. Keep to even numbers only for now, because only even numbers share exactly into two equal groups. Do not rush to the abstract number — always reach the answer by dealing real counters first, then say the number sentence.
concepts.example: You can also work backwards, which children enjoy as a puzzle: ‘Half of what number is 5?’ Deal 5 stones onto each of two plates, push them together, count 10 — ‘half of 10 is 5.’ Moving comfortably in both directions, from the whole to the half and from the half back to the whole, is a sign you truly understands.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Connect halving to doubling, which is the same fact seen from the other side. ‘Half of 8 is 4 — and look, 4 and 4 make 8.’ Lay 4 stones, then 4 more, and count all 8 together; then take one group away and say ‘half of 8 is 4.’ Seeing the two facts together (half of 8 is 4, and double 4 is 8) helps both ideas stick, and it is a lovely early taste of the addition you meet later.

concepts.title: The Symbol ½ and Everyday Halves
concepts.explanation: Finally, show the written symbol ½ and say ‘one half’ each time you see it. Explain simply that the little line means the whole has been split into equal parts. Do not expect you to write ½ neatly — recognising it and reading it as ‘one half’ is plenty for Year 1. Always tie the symbol back to a picture or an object, so ½ means something real and not just marks on a page. Point out halves in everyday life so the idea lives beyond the lesson. ‘Half past four, when we go to the masjid’ — a half of the hour. ‘Your cup is half full.’ ‘Let us have half a banana each.’ Naming these small halves through the day, again and again, does more to teach the concept than any worksheet, because you meet a half as a normal, useful, fair part of family life. ‘Any two pieces are halves.’ The most common error — you ignore size. Always ask ‘Are the two parts equal?’ Fold or match them to check. Confusing ‘two parts’ with ‘two equal parts.’ Show an obviously unequal split next to a true half so you see the difference clearly. Trying to halve odd numbers. If you try to share 5 fairly between two, one group is left with more. Let them see this, then explain that some numbers cannot be split into two equal groups — that is why we practise with even numbers. Thinking halves must be the same shape. Two equal halves of a square can be two triangles or two rectangles. Equal in size is what matters, not same in shape.
concepts.example: Reading ½ as a whole number. You may think the symbol is a normal number. Keep saying ‘one half’ and pointing to a picture of a real half.

explorations.title: What a Half Really Means (two equal parts)
explorations.context: The whole unit rests on one idea: a half is one of two equal parts. Not just two parts — two equal parts. It is easy to break a biscuit into a big bit and a tiny bit and call them ‘halves’, because there are two pieces.
explorations.prompt: If you break a biscuit into one big piece and one tiny piece, are the two pieces halves?
explorations.answer: No — the two pieces must be equal in size to be called halves.
explorations.hint: Remember the most important word: equal. Are the two pieces the same size?
explorations.explanation: Folding the anjero so the two sides sit exactly on top of each other is what proves the parts are equal — if you tear it into a big bit and a small bit instead, there are still two pieces, but neither one is a half. Keep returning to the word 'equal' every time, because that is the detail a five-year-old will happily skip if you let them.

explorations.title: Halves of Shapes (fold, cut and draw a line)
explorations.context: Now you halve shapes. The surprising part is that a shape can often be cut in half in more than one way, and every correct way still makes two equal parts.
explorations.prompt: If you cut a square from corner to corner, you get two triangles. Are the two triangles still halves?
explorations.answer: Yes — they are still halves, because the two triangles are equal in size, even though a straight cut would have made rectangles instead.
explorations.hint: Place one triangle on top of the other — do they match exactly?
explorations.explanation: A fold that lines up exactly is the proof that two parts are equal, so fold rather than just look, since looking alone can trick the eye. A circle can be halved with a line straight down, straight across, or slanted through the middle, and a square cut corner to corner still makes two halves even though the pieces are triangles rather than rectangles — different shape, same size, still a half.

explorations.title: Half of a Set (share a group equally between two)
explorations.context: A half is not only for shapes — it works for groups of objects too. To find half of a set, you share the group equally between two. Each of the two groups then holds the same number, and that number is ‘half of’ the whole set.
explorations.prompt: Share 6 dates equally between two plates, dealing one at a time. How many dates end up on each plate?
explorations.hint: Deal them one at a time, back and forth: one for this plate, one for that plate...
explorations.explanation: Dealing objects one at a time, back and forth onto two plates, is what guarantees a fair share — if you grab handfuls instead, the two piles are unlikely to match. Once both plates hold the same number, that number is 'half of' the whole set, which connects this new idea straight back to counting, something you already do well.

explorations.title: Halving Small Even Numbers
explorations.context: From sharing real objects, you move to halving numbers: half of 2 is 1, half of 4 is 2, half of 6 is 3, half of 8 is 4, half of 10 is 5. Keep to even numbers only for now, because only even numbers share exactly into two equal groups.
explorations.hint: Share 8 counters equally between two plates, then count how many are on one plate.
explorations.explanation: Half of 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 (1, 2, 3, 4 and 5) should always come from dealing out real counters first, not from memorising the answer — the number sentence is simply the label for what you have just shared out fairly. Halving also connects to doubling: if half of 8 is 4, then 4 and 4 together make 8 again, so the two facts check each other.

explorations.title: The Symbol ½ and Everyday Halves
explorations.context: Finally, show the written symbol ½ and say ‘one half’ each time you see it. Explain simply that the little line means the whole has been split into equal parts.
explorations.prompt: What do we say when we see the symbol ½?
explorations.hint: Think of the little line splitting one whole into two equal parts.
explorations.explanation: Say 'one half' every time you see the symbol ½, and tie it straight back to something real, such as half an orange, so the mark on the page never floats free of meaning. Pointing out halves you already meets in daily life, like 'half past four', shows that this new piece of maths is a word they already use, not just a page in a workbook.

explorations.title: What a Half Really Means (two equal parts)
explorations.context: The whole unit rests on one idea: a half is one of two equal parts. Not just two parts — two equal parts. It is easy to break a biscuit into a big bit and a tiny bit and call them ‘halves’, because there are two pieces.
explorations.prompt: You fold a shape in half and the two sides match exactly, with nothing sticking out. Are the two parts equal or not equal?
explorations.hint: A fold that lines up perfectly on both sides means the parts match in size.
explorations.explanation: Look at each shape here and check two things: does the dividing line pass through the true middle, and would folding the two sides make them match exactly? That test is what decides 'equal' or 'not equal' — not how many pieces there are, since an unevenly split shape still has two parts, it just does not have two halves.

methods.title: Fold to Make Two Equal Halves
methods.example: Folding a paper circle to check for two equal halves
steps: Take one whole shape, such as a paper circle or a piece of anjero, and hold it flat.
Fold it carefully so one side lies exactly on top of the other side.
Check that the two folded sides match exactly — if they do, you have made two halves.

methods.title: Check Two Parts Are Really Equal
methods.example: Comparing two cut pieces of bread to see if they match
steps: Cut or tear a whole, such as a piece of bread, into two parts.
Place one part directly on top of the other part.
If the edges line up exactly with nothing sticking out, the parts are equal halves; if one part is bigger, they are not halves.

methods.title: Spot Equal Parts vs Unequal Parts
methods.example: Looking at two cut shapes and deciding if they are halves
steps: Look at a shape that has been cut into two parts.
Compare the size of the two parts by placing them side by side or on top of each other.
Say 'equal parts' if they match exactly, or 'unequal parts' if one piece is bigger than the other.

methods.title: Draw a Line to Make Two Halves
methods.example: Drawing a line through the middle of a square
steps: Look at the shape and find its middle point.
Draw one straight line through the middle so it splits the shape into two parts.
Fold along your line to check that both parts are exactly the same size.

methods.title: Find Different Ways to Halve One Shape
methods.example: Halving a square straight down, straight across, and corner to corner
steps: Take one square or circle shape and draw a line to make two halves.
Now draw a different line through the same shape — a new way to split it into two equal parts.
Check each new line still makes two equal parts by folding or measuring; both ways are still 'halves'.

methods.title: Join Two Halves to Remake the Whole
methods.example: Pushing two half-circles back together to make one whole circle
steps: Take your two half pieces from a shape you have just halved.
Push the two straight edges together so they line up exactly.
Check that the joined shape looks like the original whole again.

workedExamples.title: Is It a Half?
workedExamples.prompt: Amina has one anjero. She tears it into two pieces — one big piece and one small piece. Are these two pieces halves?
workedExamples.solution: No. A half must be one of two EQUAL parts. Amina's two pieces are not the same size, so they are not halves. To make halves, she should fold the anjero in half first to find the middle, then tear along the fold. Now both pieces are the same size, so each piece is a half.

workedExamples.title: Do the Two Halves Match?
workedExamples.prompt: Yusuf cuts an orange into two pieces. He puts one piece on top of the other and they line up exactly, with nothing sticking out. What does this tell him?
workedExamples.solution: Because the two pieces line up exactly with no part sticking out, they are the same size. This means Yusuf has cut the orange into two equal halves. If any part had stuck out, the pieces would not be equal, and they would not be halves.

workedExamples.title: Equal or Unequal?
workedExamples.prompt: A chapati is cut into two pieces: one piece is a big half-circle and the other is a tiny sliver. Are the two pieces equal parts or unequal parts?
workedExamples.solution: The two pieces are unequal parts, because one piece is much bigger than the other. For the pieces to be equal (halves), they need to be exactly the same size. Ask: 'Would each of us be happy with either piece?' If not, the parts are unequal.

workedExamples.title: Which Shows a Half?
workedExamples.prompt: Look at two circles. Circle A has a straight line through the middle, making two matching parts. Circle B has a line near the edge, making one big part and one tiny part. Which circle shows a half?
workedExamples.solution: Circle A shows a half, because its line goes through the middle and makes two equal parts. Circle B does not show a half, because its line is off to one side, making one part much bigger than the other.

workedExamples.title: Halving One Shape Two Ways
workedExamples.prompt: Fatima has one square piece of paper. Show two different ways she can fold it to make two halves.
workedExamples.solution: Way 1: fold the square in half from top to bottom, making two equal rectangles. Way 2: fold the square in half from corner to corner, making two equal triangles. Both ways give two equal parts, so both are correct ways to make halves — a shape can be halved in more than one way.

workedExamples.title: Putting the Halves Back Together
workedExamples.prompt: Hodan cuts a round biscuit into two equal halves. How can she check the two pieces really are halves of the same whole biscuit?
workedExamples.solution: Hodan pushes the two straight cut edges back together. If the pieces fit back together perfectly and make the same round biscuit shape as before, with no gaps or overlaps, then the two pieces are true halves.

workedExamples.title: Sharing Six Dates Equally
workedExamples.prompt: There are 6 dates and 2 plates. Share the dates equally between the two plates. How many dates end up on each plate?
workedExamples.solution: Deal the dates one at a time, back and forth: one for this plate, one for that plate, and so on until all 6 dates are shared. Each plate ends up with 3 dates. So half of 6 dates is 3 — each plate has the same amount, which is fair.

workedExamples.title: Half of 8
workedExamples.prompt: Colour one half of each shape, making the two parts equal. Then work out: what is half of 8 stones shared between two children?
workedExamples.solution: First, share 8 stones equally between two children: deal them one at a time until each child has the same number. Each child gets 4 stones. So half of 8 is 4. Check: 4 and 4 together make 8 again.

workedExamples.title: Halving Different Shapes: Triangle, Oval, Diamond
workedExamples.prompt: Look at a triangle, an oval, and a diamond. Which of these can be folded to show two equal halves?
workedExamples.solution: All three shapes can be folded into two equal halves if you fold along the right line: fold the oval down its long middle line, fold the diamond corner to corner, and fold the triangle from its top point straight down to the middle of its base. In each case, check the two folded sides match exactly to confirm they are true halves.

workedExamples.title: Checking a Tricky Half
workedExamples.prompt: Ibrahim folds a rectangle, but the fold is a little off to one side, so one part looks slightly bigger. Is this a half? What should Ibrahim do?
workedExamples.solution: This is not a half yet, because the two parts are not exactly equal. Ibrahim should unfold the paper, find the true middle by measuring or folding edge to edge, and fold again exactly at the middle. Only when both parts match exactly can he call them halves.

workedExamples.title: Sorting Equal and Unequal Cuts
workedExamples.prompt: Look at four cut shapes. Two show two equal parts and two show two unequal parts. How can you sort them correctly?
workedExamples.solution: For each shape, fold or place one part on top of the other. If the parts match exactly with no overlap or gap, sort it into 'equal parts (halves)'. If one part is bigger than the other, sort it into 'unequal parts (not halves)'.

workedExamples.title: Half of a Number: Finding Half of 10
workedExamples.prompt: Deal 10 stones onto two plates, one at a time, until they are shared equally. What is half of 10?
workedExamples.solution: Dealing 10 stones one at a time between two plates gives 5 stones on each plate. Since both plates have the same amount, half of 10 is 5. Check: 5 and 5 together make 10 again.

practice.prompt: Look at a circle cut into two matching pieces. Is each piece a whole or a half?
practice.answer: Each piece is a half, because the circle has been cut into two equal parts.
practice.hint: A half is one of two EQUAL parts — check that the pieces match.

practice.prompt: A banana is cut into two pieces: one long piece and one short piece. Are these two pieces halves?
practice.answer: No, they are not halves, because the two pieces are not equal in size.
practice.hint: Compare the sizes of the two pieces — do they match?

practice.prompt: Fold a square piece of paper so the two sides match exactly. What have you made?
practice.answer: You have made two halves of the square.
practice.hint: Fold so both sides line up exactly, with no part sticking out.

practice.prompt: Look at two shapes: Shape A has a line through its middle making two equal parts. Shape B has a line making one big part and one small part. Which shape shows a half?
practice.hint: Look for the shape with two parts that match exactly.

practice.prompt: Circle the shapes that are cut into two equal parts: a circle cut straight down the middle, a square cut near one edge, and a rectangle cut straight across the middle.
practice.answer: The circle cut down the middle and the rectangle cut across the middle are cut into two equal parts; the square cut near one edge is not.
practice.hint: Check whether the cutting line goes through the middle of the shape.

practice.prompt: Look at four shapes marked with different cuts. Say 'equal' if the two parts match, or 'not equal' if they do not.
practice.answer: Say 'equal' for shapes cut exactly through the middle, and 'not equal' for shapes cut off to one side.
practice.hint: Fold or compare the two parts of each shape to check if they match.

practice.prompt: Colour one half of a circle red. How much of the circle should stay uncoloured?
practice.answer: Half of the circle should stay uncoloured, because the whole circle is split into two equal halves.
practice.hint: Halves are equal — the coloured part and the uncoloured part must match in size.

practice.prompt: Colour one half of each shape: a square, a rectangle, and a triangle. Make sure the two parts of each shape are equal.
practice.answer: For each shape, colour exactly one of the two equal parts, leaving the other equal part uncoloured.
practice.hint: First find the line that splits each shape into two matching parts, then colour one side.

practice.prompt: Look at a triangle, an oval, and a diamond. Which lines would cut each shape into two equal halves?
practice.answer: The oval is halved by a line down its long middle; the diamond is halved corner to corner; the triangle is halved by a line from its top point to the middle of its base.
practice.hint: Look for the line that makes both parts match when folded.

practice.prompt: Share 8 mangoes equally between two baskets. How many mangoes are in each basket?
practice.answer: Each basket gets 4 mangoes, because half of 8 is 4.
practice.hint: Deal the mangoes one at a time, back and forth, into the two baskets.

practice.prompt: Half of a number is 3. What is the whole number?
practice.answer: The whole number is 6, because half of 6 is 3 (3 and 3 make 6).
practice.hint: Think of the doubling fact: half of what number gives 3?

practice.prompt: Find half of a number: half of 2, half of 4, half of 6, half of 8, and half of 10.
practice.answer: Half of 2 is 1, half of 4 is 2, half of 6 is 3, half of 8 is 4, and half of 10 is 5.
practice.hint: Share each number equally between two plates using real objects if you need to check.

activities.title: Practise together
activities.materials: Paper, pencil and familiar household objects
steps: Choose one idea from this unit.
Build or draw a model of it.
Explain your model to a family member.
Write one question of your own and solve it.

commonMistakes: A common mistake is picking the biscuit with the big and tiny pieces just because there are two pieces
Remember that two pieces only count as halves if they are the SAME size.

fluency.prompt: Point to the object that has been cut into a half: a biscuit broken into two same-size pieces, or a biscuit broken into one big piece and one tiny piece.
fluency.answer: The biscuit broken into two same-size pieces shows a half.
fluency.hint: A half means the two pieces must be equal.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is picking the biscuit with the big and tiny pieces just because there are two pieces. Remember that two pieces only count as halves if they are the SAME size.

fluency.prompt: True or false: the two halves of a whole must always be the exact same size.
fluency.hint: Think about what makes two parts 'equal'.
fluency.errorFeedback: You might say 'false', thinking any two pieces count as halves. Correct this by folding a shape and showing that only matching folds count as equal halves.

fluency.prompt: A rope is cut into two pieces: one is much longer than the other. Are these two pieces equal parts or unequal parts?
fluency.hint: Compare the lengths of the two pieces.
fluency.errorFeedback: You might say 'equal parts' just because there are two pieces. Correct this by placing the two rope pieces side by side to show one is clearly longer.

fluency.prompt: Which line correctly cuts a rectangle into two halves: a line straight down the middle, or a line near one short edge?
fluency.answer: The line straight down the middle.
fluency.hint: The halving line must pass through the middle of the shape.
fluency.errorFeedback: You might pick the line near the edge because it still makes two pieces. Correct this by folding along each line and comparing the two resulting parts.

fluency.prompt: A circle can be halved with a line straight down, straight across, or slanted through the middle. True or false: only one of these ways is correct?
fluency.answer: False — all three ways are correct, as long as the line passes through the middle.
fluency.hint: Think about how many different lines can pass through the centre of a circle.
fluency.errorFeedback: You might think only a straight-down cut counts. Correct this by demonstrating that any line through the centre of a circle makes two equal halves.

fluency.prompt: You have two half-circles from the same circle. What should happen when you push their straight edges together?
fluency.answer: They should fit together perfectly and remake the original whole circle.
fluency.hint: The two halves came from one whole, so they should match up exactly.
fluency.errorFeedback: You might push mismatched halves together and not notice gaps. Correct this by checking the curved edges line up all the way around when the halves are joined.

fluency.prompt: Share 4 sweets equally between two children. How many sweets does each child get?
fluency.hint: Deal the sweets one at a time, back and forth.
fluency.errorFeedback: You might give 3 to one and 1 to the other because it is faster. Correct this by dealing one at a time so both children end up with the same number.

fluency.hint: Share 6 counters equally between two groups.
fluency.errorFeedback: You might answer 6, forgetting to halve, or guess 4. Correct this by dealing 6 counters one at a time onto two plates and counting each plate: 3 and 3.

fluency.prompt: What do we call the symbol ½?
fluency.hint: Look at the two numbers in the symbol — one whole split into two equal parts.
fluency.errorFeedback: You might read it as 'one two' without meaning. Correct this by connecting the symbol to a real half, such as half an orange, every time it appears.

fluency.prompt: Review: what makes two parts halves of a whole?
fluency.answer: The two parts must be equal — the same size or amount.
fluency.hint: Remember the most important word from this whole unit: equal.
fluency.errorFeedback: You might say 'two parts' is enough. Correct this by reminding them that equal size is what makes parts halves, not just having two pieces.

fluency.prompt: Look at a whole apple cut into two matching pieces. What is each piece called?
fluency.answer: Each piece is called a half.
fluency.hint: One of two equal parts of a whole is called a half.
fluency.errorFeedback: You might call each piece 'a whole' since it is a real object on its own. Correct this by reminding them the original apple was the whole, and each equal piece is now a half of it.

fluency.hint: Share 2 counters equally between two plates.
fluency.errorFeedback: You might answer 2, forgetting to share. Correct this by dealing 2 counters one at a time onto two plates: 1 and 1.

realProblems.prompt: At home, Amina has one chapati for breakfast. She wants to share it fairly with her little brother so they each get a half. How should she cut it?
realProblems.answer: Amina should fold the chapati in half first to find the middle, then cut along the fold so both pieces are exactly the same size — each piece is a half.
realProblems.hint: Fold first to find the exact middle before cutting.
realProblems.errorFeedback: You might cut without folding first and end up with an uneven cut. Correct this by folding to find the middle before cutting, so both halves match.

realProblems.prompt: At the market, a trader cuts a watermelon into two pieces to sell as halves. One piece looks bigger than the other. Can the trader call both pieces halves?
realProblems.answer: No — since the pieces are not the same size, they are not true halves. The trader should cut through the middle so both pieces are equal before calling them halves.
realProblems.hint: Halves must be equal in size, not just two pieces from one melon.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A buyer, or child, might accept any two pieces as 'halves' just because there are two. Correct this by comparing the two pieces side by side to check they truly match.

realProblems.prompt: On a journey, a family has one bottle of water. They pour it into two cups, but one cup is much fuller than the other. Are the two cups holding equal parts or unequal parts of the water?
realProblems.answer: Unequal parts — one cup has more water than the other.
realProblems.hint: Compare how full each cup is.
realProblems.errorFeedback: You might assume two cups automatically means equal sharing. Correct this by pouring carefully and checking the water level in each cup matches before calling them equal.

realProblems.prompt: Grandmother bakes one round loaf of bread and cuts it into two equal pieces to share with a neighbour. What is each piece called?
realProblems.answer: Each piece is called a half, because the loaf has been cut into two equal parts.
realProblems.hint: Recall: a half is one of two equal parts of a whole.
realProblems.errorFeedback: You might call the pieces 'two wholes' since each looks like separate food. Correct this by reminding them the loaf was one whole first, so each equal piece is a half of it.

realProblems.prompt: A father tells his two children, 'Half past four we will go to the masjid.' What does 'half' mean in 'half past four'?
realProblems.answer: It means 30 minutes, which is half of the 60 minutes in one hour — halfway between four o’clock and five o’clock.
realProblems.hint: Think about halves of time, just like halves of shapes and sets.
realProblems.errorFeedback: You might think 'half past' means a random extra bit of time. Correct this by showing a clock: halfway between the 4 and the 5 is 'half past four'.

realProblems.prompt: A mother has 10 dates and wants to share them equally between her two children so each gets half. How many dates does each child get?
realProblems.answer: Each child gets 5 dates, because half of 10 is 5.
realProblems.hint: Deal the dates one at a time between the two children.
realProblems.errorFeedback: You might split them unevenly, like 6 and 4, because it is faster. Correct this by dealing one at a time, back and forth, until all 10 are shared equally.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why colouring 'one half' of a shape means colouring exactly one of two equal parts, not just some of the shape.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: When you colour one half of a shape, you must first split the whole shape into two equal parts. Then you colour only one of those two parts. If the two parts are not equal, colouring one of them is not really colouring 'a half' — it might be more or less than half.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why must the two parts of a shape be equal before you can call one of them 'a half'?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: If the two parts are not equal, one part is bigger and one is smaller, so neither part is truly half of the whole. Only when both parts are the same size — equal — can each one correctly be called a half.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Look at a triangle cut into two unequal pieces. Explain how you can tell the pieces are not halves, and what the fraction word 'half' actually means.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: You can tell the pieces are not halves by comparing their sizes — if you fold or place one on the other and they don't match, they are unequal, not equal. A fraction is a part of a whole, and 'half' is a special fraction that only applies when a whole is split into two parts that are exactly equal.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Halving Small Even Numbers.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: To halve a small even number, share it equally between two groups: half of 2 is 1, half of 4 is 2, half of 6 is 3, half of 8 is 4, and half of 10 is 5. Halving connects to doubling — if half of 8 is 4, then 4 and 4 together make 8 again.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in The Symbol ½ and Everyday Halves.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The symbol ½ is read as 'one half' and means a whole has been split into two equal parts. We see halves in everyday life too, like 'half past four' meaning 30 minutes past four o'clock — halfway to five o'clock.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in What a Half Really Means (two equal parts).
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A half is one of two EQUAL parts of a whole — not just any two pieces. For example, if you fold a piece of anjero so the two sides match exactly, each side is a half. If one side is bigger than the other, the pieces are not halves.

questions.question: Which line cuts a square into two halves: a line straight through the middle, or a line close to one edge?
options: A line straight through the middle
A line close to one edge
Any line at all
There is no correct line
questions.answer: A line straight through the middle
questions.hint: The line must pass through the middle so both parts match.
questions.explanation: A shape is cut into halves by a line through its middle, making two equal parts.

questions.question: A circle can be halved with a line straight down, straight across, or slanted through the middle. Is more than one of these ways correct?

No, only a straight-down line is correct
No, only a straight-across line is correct
No shape can be halved more than one way
questions.answer: Yes, any line through the middle makes two equal halves
questions.hint: Think about how many lines can pass through the centre of a circle.
questions.explanation: A shape can often be halved in more than one way, as long as each line passes through the middle and makes two equal parts.

questions.question: You have two halves that came from the same whole circle. What should happen when you push them back together?
options: They fit together perfectly and remake the whole circle
They leave a gap in the middle
They overlap each other
They make a different shape
questions.answer: They fit together perfectly and remake the whole circle
questions.hint: Two true halves always remake their original whole.
questions.explanation: Because the two pieces are equal halves of the same whole, pushing them together remakes the original whole shape exactly.

rounds.prompt: What is half of 10?
rounds.clue: Deal 10 counters one at a time onto two plates.
rounds.explanation: Half of 10 is 5, because sharing 10 equally between two plates gives 5 on each plate.

selfAssessment: I can say that a half is one of two equal parts of a whole.
I can understand that the two halves must be equal in size or amount.
I can tell the difference between equal parts and unequal parts.
I can fold or draw a line to cut a shape into two halves.
I can see that a shape can often be halved in more than one way.
I can put two halves back together to remake the whole.
I can share a small group of objects equally between two to find half of a set.
I can find half of small even numbers: half of 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.
